Formulation:
Predisposing: Possible trait anxiety; family history of chronic illness (mother with migraines) may heighten vigilance to bodily sensations.  
Precipitating: Sudden onset of severe unilateral headache with visual aura and vomiting.  
Perpetuating: Catastrophic misinterpretation of physical symptoms (“brain tumour,” “stroke”); limited prior experience with migraines.  
Protective: Motivated to understand condition; receptive to education; intact insight; no evidence of mood disorder or self-harm thoughts.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Health anxiety / illness-related worry
- Patient Goal(s): Understand and manage anxiety about physical symptoms; feel reassured about current health; develop strategies to reduce catastrophic thinking.
- Clinical Goal(s): Provide psycho-education on migraine; screen for anxiety disorder; teach brief anxiety-management techniques; consider CBT referral if anxiety persists.
- Actions (Patient):
  • Read provided material on migraine and common physical symptoms of anxiety.  
  • Practice paced breathing when feeling worried.  
  • Monitor anxiety levels and triggers in diary until review.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  • Offer brief explanation of migraine pathophysiology and typical course.  
  • Provide written resources on health anxiety and coping strategies.  
  • Arrange follow-up appointment after headache assessment to review anxiety; administer GAD-7 or similar screening tool.  
  • Consider referral to psychologist for CBT if clinically indicated.

Secondary Problem: First-episode probable migraine with aura
- Patient Goal(s): Achieve pain relief; reduce nausea; understand when to seek urgent care.
- Clinical Goal(s): Symptom control; confirm migraine diagnosis; rule out serious intracranial pathology if atypical features develop.
- Actions (Patient):
  • Trial ibuprofen with anti-emetic and hydration/sugary carbonated drink as advised.  
  • Rest in dark room; avoid screen exposure.  
  • Attend scheduled in-person assessment; seek emergency care if sudden worsening, neurological deficit, or “worst ever” headache occurs.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  • Provide clear medication regimen (dose/route/frequency to be determined at pharmacy).  
  • Book same-day face-to-face review for neurological examination.  
  • Escalate for imaging/ED referral if red-flag symptoms emerge.

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered: Migraine features and management; distinction between migraine and life-threatening causes; initial coping techniques for anxiety.
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Sudden escalation in headache severity; new neurological deficits; persistent high anxiety interfering with function.
- Coping Strategies: Breathing exercises, rest in low-stimulus environment, gradual exposure to reassurance-seeking reduction, self-monitoring diary.

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Yes (verbal during consultation).
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: To be provided electronically.
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: None currently.
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not applicable.
- Review Date: Within 2–4 weeks or sooner if symptoms escalate.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Migraine with aura – High likelihood. Classic unilateral headache with visual aura, nausea/vomiting, family history. 
- Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Medium likelihood. Sudden “first” headache warrants exclusion despite lower pain rating and no neuro-deficit.
- Cervical/vertebral artery dissection – Low–Medium likelihood. Unilateral headache and visual disturbance but lacks trauma/neck pain.
